memoryTip: Think magnum (huge bottle) — magnitude is how big or important something is.
correctPassage: Few grasped the magnitude of the problem until the report was published.
wrongPassages: He praised the magnitude of a speck of dust on the microscope lens.
The magnitude of her whisper filled every seat in the open stadium.
They ranked magnitude by how friendly the clerk seemed at checkout.

memoryTip: Epitome = the perfect example; to epitomize is to be that example.
correctPassage: The building’s spare lines epitomize mid-century modern design.
wrongPassages: The messy draft epitomized polish after three rounds of careful editing.
His empty calendar epitomized a week packed with back-to-back meetings.
They said the rusty bike epitomized a brand-new product launch.

definition: failure to meet an obligation; or a preselected option
memoryTip: If you don’t choose, you get the default — the fallback (or you fail to pay).
correctPassage: If no option is selected, the software uses a conservative default setting.
wrongPassages: She defaulted the speech with vivid stories that held the room’s attention.
His default honesty meant he never stuck to a single story twice.
They chose the default option by carefully comparing every alternative first.

definition: unnecessary; more than what is needed
memoryTip: Super + flow — overflow you don’t need; extra fluff to cut.
correctPassage: Editors cut superfluous adjectives that added length without clarity.
wrongPassages: Water is superfluous for desert plants that must drink daily to survive.
The pilot called the checklist superfluous moments before using every item on it.
Her superfluous notes were the only reason anyone passed the exam.

definition: the quality of being exact; precision
memoryTip: Exact + -itude — the state of being exact; pure precision.
correctPassage: Cartography of that era prized exactitude over decorative flourish.
wrongPassages: He praised the exactitude of a guess that landed miles from the true value.
Her exactitude with dates meant she routinely mixed up years and names.
They aimed for exactitude by rounding every measurement to the nearest hundred.

memoryTip: En-gender: “give birth to” an idea, feeling, or result — cause it.
correctPassage: Poor communication can engender distrust between teams.
wrongPassages: Extra safety checks engendered the risk by stripping every warning label.
They engendered the empty warehouse by hauling every crate out overnight.
Her silence engendered the rumor by answering every question in full.

definition: officially assign a status, role, or name
memoryTip: De-sign it as official — name or assign a role on purpose.
correctPassage: The city will designate several blocks as a historic district.
wrongPassages: He designated the secret hideout by never writing its name anywhere.
She designated the captain by refusing to name anyone at all.
They designated the winner by drawing lots and then ignoring the result.

definition: make an unpleasant feeling less intense
memoryTip: Sounds like “a suage / soothe age of pain” — ease a bad feeling.
correctPassage: A public apology did little to assuage anger over the spill.
wrongPassages: His jokes only assuaged the tension by making everyone angrier.
They assuaged the shortage by shipping even less grain next month.
She assuaged her thirst by locking the water bottle in a drawer.

definition: a made-up falsehood; or the act of manufacturing
memoryTip: Fabricated like fake cloth — a made-up story (or something manufactured).
correctPassage: The diary entry later proved to be a fabrication invented for publicity.
wrongPassages: The live video feed was a fabrication that matched every timestamp on the clock.
Her fabrication of the recipe meant she followed the cookbook word for word.
They called the signed contract a fabrication after both sides had just signed it.

memoryTip: In earnest — sincere, not joking; you really mean it.
correctPassage: In an earnest letter, she asked the board to reconsider the cuts.
wrongPassages: His earnest promise lasted until the door closed and he laughed it off.
She gave an earnest shrug that made clear she did not care at all.
The earnest flyer advertised a free trip, then buried a $900 fee in fine print.
